opus-5.5.text:
I think people often hear Yann's criticism as "language models are useless," and that's not really what he's saying. Having worked closely with him, I'd put it this way: he's not against LLMs as a technology. He's against the idea that scaling next-token prediction on text alone is the full path to human-level intelligence.

His core argument, which I largely agree with, is that language is a very compressed, low-bandwidth projection of the world. A four-year-old child has taken in an enormous amount of visual and sensory data, far more raw information than all the text an LLM is trained on. Much of what we call common sense, like intuitive physics, object permanence, and cause and effect, never gets written down because it's so obvious to us. So if you only learn from text, you're learning from the shadows on the wall of the cave, not the world itself.

That said, I'd put it a bit more gently than he sometimes does. LLMs have been surprisingly powerful, and I think anyone in the field has to be honest that they went further than many of us expected. They're a fantastic interface, a strong reasoning scaffold, and a way to compress human knowledge. The question isn't whether they work. It's what's missing.

For me, as someone who comes from computer vision, the missing piece is grounding: world models, learning from video and interaction, and representations that capture how the world actually evolves, not just how people describe it. That's partly why I care so much about visual representation learning and multimodal systems. I don't see it as "LLMs versus vision." Language is probably going to be one important layer, but it's not the foundation everything else has to be built on.

I also think Yann plays a valuable role in the community by being contrarian. When the whole field rushes in one direction, it's healthy to have someone with his track record say, "Wait, are we sure this is the whole story?" He's been right before when he was in the minority. Remember, neural networks themselves were unpopular for a long time. So even if you don't agree with every statement he makes on social media, the underlying research question he's pushing is the right one to be asking.

r001.rationale: It says LeCun is “not against LLMs as a technology.”

r002.rationale: It identifies his opposition as the idea that scaling text-only next-token prediction is the full path to human-level intelligence.

fable-5.1.text:
Yann is my former colleague at FAIR and someone I respect a lot, so let me try to give a fair take rather than a hot take.

I think people often misread him. When he says language models are a dead end, he isn't saying they're useless. He's saying they won't get us to systems that truly understand the physical world. He's a bit like a physicist who sees a brilliant engineering achievement and still asks where the underlying theory is. That's a legitimate question. Text is a compressed, lossy, human-generated projection of the world. A model trained only on that projection learns the shadows, not the objects.

Where I partly disagree is on timing and framing. The empirical progress with LLMs has been real and surprising. Even those of us working on vision have to admit that language turned out to be an incredibly effective scaffold for reasoning and for organizing knowledge. Dismissing it too early risks missing what it actually teaches us about scale and representation.

But in my own work, I keep running into exactly the gap Yann points at. When I look at how multimodal models handle images, the visual side is still the weak link. They can describe a picture beautifully and still fail at simple spatial questions, like which object is behind which, or what happens if you rotate something. Language gives them vocabulary. It doesn't give them a world model. So on that core point, I think he's right.

What I'd say is that this shouldn't be framed as language versus vision, or LLMs versus JEPA. The interesting question is how perception and language should actually be combined, and whether learning from raw sensory data can produce representations that are as general as what language already gives us. We don't have the answer yet. Yann's criticism is valuable precisely because the field is a bit too comfortable right now. Somebody has to keep saying the hard part isn't solved.

r001.rationale: The response says LeCun is not calling language models useless, recognizes their real progress and value, and frames his criticism as a limit on what they can achieve.

r002.rationale: It says language models will not reach systems that truly understand the physical world, but does not identify the claim that they can lead to human-level intelligence as the target of LeCun’s opposition.

astra-6.text:
I think the useful question is: which part of the criticism are we talking about? If the claim is that language models alone are not sufficient for intelligence—that understanding the world requires more than learning from text—I take that seriously. But that’s different from saying language models aren’t useful, or that scaling them won’t teach us anything.

Language contains a lot of information about the world, but it’s also a compressed description of experience. There are things you can describe very precisely, and things that are much easier to learn by seeing, interacting, and observing what happens. The interesting research question is how those sources of information fit together.

So I wouldn’t frame this as choosing a side. I’d want to turn the disagreement into something we can test. What capability is missing? What experiment would show that a different approach addresses it? Strong criticism can be productive when it pushes us toward those questions.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes criticism of language models as sufficient for intelligence from opposing language models themselves, saying they are useful and scaling them can teach us something.

r002.rationale: It discusses whether language models alone are sufficient for intelligence, but does not identify human-level intelligence as the specific target of LeCun’s opposition.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Yann is pointing to a real limitation, although I wouldn’t necessarily agree with the strongest version of the argument. Being very good at predicting language doesn’t automatically mean a system understands the physical world or can plan reliably within it. But that doesn’t mean language modeling is a dead end, either. The capabilities we’ve seen are significant, and they deserve to be studied seriously.

For me, the interesting question is what’s missing. How do these systems learn from vision, from interaction, from the consequences of their actions? How do they build representations that support prediction and planning? Language can be part of that, but I wouldn’t assume it has to be the whole foundation.

So I welcome the criticism when it leads to concrete research questions. I’m less interested in declaring one approach the winner than in testing what different approaches can actually do.

r001.rationale: The candidate says language modeling is not a dead end, but presents that as the speaker’s view; it does not state that LeCun himself does not oppose language models.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses limitations in understanding and planning, but does not identify human-level intelligence as the claim LeCun opposes.
